results.summary: This project is a Verilog implementation of the 74HC595 8-bit serial-in, parallel-out shift register with output latches. It accepts serial data, shift clock, latch clock, output enable and clear inputs, and drives eight parallel outputs. It is tested by connecting eight LEDs, such as a Pmod LED board, and bit-banging data from a host. The author confirmed working silicon by creating a Knight Rider effect with C and MicroPython programs.

This design is an HLS implementation of the NIST 800.22 Monobit test for evaluating whether a bit source is random. It samples one input bit per clock and produces a valid pulse and an is_random result every 65536 cycles. The design needs only a clock and an input bit, with no external hardware currently required. The documentation notes that external hardware is planned but not yet added, and the test interval is fixed.

This project plays the Super Mario theme through a piezo speaker connected across two output pins. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and plays it back using differential PWM modulation. The design requires a roughly 3 kHz clock on one input and a brief reset pulse on another to start playback. It is a small audio demo with no silicon test report provided.

This project converts an 8-bit binary input into signals for a 7-segment hexadecimal display. The documentation consists only of placeholder text, so the exact mapping and behavior cannot be confirmed from the provided material. It is a Wokwi project with eight input pins and eight output pins. No test procedure or external hardware requirements are described.

LaRVa is a RISC-V CPU design with a serial port, several peripherals, and a JTAG interface. It requires external SRAM memory and address latches attached to the PMOD connectors, and includes a bootloader that loads programs over the serial port. Testing starts by sending an 'L' over a 115200 bps serial link and checking for the bootloader reply. The design is documented in accompanying PDF files and targets a 24 MHz clock.

This project implements a 4-bit successive approximation analog-to-digital converter in an analog Tiny Tapeout tile. It takes an analog input on ua[0], requires a 5 MHz clock, and produces an end-of-conversion signal plus four digital output bits. Each conversion takes five clock cycles, giving a 1 MHz conversion rate, and the input must be held constant by an external sample-and-hold circuit. The reset must be pulsed after each end-of-conversion signal, and no silicon test results are reported.

This is a simple one-stage RISC-V CPU based on a university lecture. Instructions are 32 bits wide but are loaded over four clock cycles through an 8-bit input bus, and the ALU result is exposed on the output pins. The design is verified with a testbench containing simple instructions, and the documentation notes that the chip is not being shipped at this time. No external hardware is required for the described testing.

This is a factory test module for TinyTapeout 05. When input 0 is high it outputs a toggling counter on both the output and bidirectional pins; otherwise it mirrors the inputs to the outputs. It is tested by setting input 0 high and checking that the outputs toggle. The design is small, has no external hardware requirements, and is intended for manufacturing validation.

This project implements an 8-bit Concurrent Built-In Logic Block Observer for memory test. It combines AND and XOR gates, D flip-flops, and multiplexers to form a multi-stage shift register with internal feedback and observation paths. The design is intended to be verified with a testbench that exercises shifting and feedback behavior across all stages. No external hardware is required, and no silicon test results are reported.

This project displays a user-selectable Latin character on a 7-segment display. Six DIP inputs select a character code covering a-z, space, underscore, hyphen, dot, exclamation mark, and quotation mark, and the display is driven one segment at a time. A high clock rate is needed to see the character, and the documentation warns that a single lit segment indicates a clock problem. Silicon test reports from both the author and an independent tester confirm it works as intended.
